claim: The distribution of fitness effects (DFE) defines how new mutations spread through an evolving population.
source: The distribution of fitness effects (DFE) defines how new mutations spread through an evolving population.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but represents established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous mutations (dN/dS) has become a popular method to detect selection in somatic cells.
source: The ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous mutations (dN/dS) has become a popular method to detect selection in somatic cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established practice in the field, as evidenced by the citations provided later in the introduction.

claim: The link between dN/dS values and fitness coefficients in somatic evolution is missing.
source: However the link, in somatic evolution, between dN/dS values and fitness coefficients is missing.
evidence: This is a gap in knowledge identified by the authors as motivation for their study.

claim: This study presents a quantitative model of somatic evolutionary dynamics that determines the selective coefficients of individual driver mutations from dN/dS estimates.
source: Here we present a quantitative model of somatic evolutionary dynamics that determines the selective coefficients of individual driver mutations from dN/dS estimates.
evidence: This is the primary methodological contribution claimed by the authors, developed throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study measures the DFE for somatic mutant clones in ostensibly normal oesophagus and skin.
source: We then measure the DFE for somatic mutant clones in ostensibly normal oesophagus and skin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: The study reveals a broad distribution of fitness effects.
source: We reveal a broad distribution of fitness effects, with the largest fitness increases found for TP53 and NOTCH1 mutants (proliferative bias 1–5%).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: TP53 and NOTCH1 mutants have the largest fitness increases with proliferative bias of 1-5%.
source: We reveal a broad distribution of fitness effects, with the largest fitness increases found for TP53 and NOTCH1 mutants (proliferative bias 1–5%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding supported by the interval dN/dS analysis presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Measurement of the selective advantage of each driver mutation enables prediction of future evolutionary dynamics, provided the selective regime remains constant.
source: Measurement of the selective advantage of each driver mutation enables prediction of future evolutionary dynamics (Williams et al., 2019), provided the selective regime remains constant.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In somatic evolution, particularly in cancer genomes, there is extensive knowledge of the catalogue of recurrent, and likely positively selected, somatic mutations.
source: In somatic evolution, particularly in cancer genomes, we have an extensive knowledge of the catalogue of recurrent, and likely positively selected, somatic mutations (Martincorena et al., 2017), but the fitness changes associated with each mutation remain largely unquantified.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Martincorena et al., 2017.

claim: The fitness changes associated with each mutation in somatic evolution remain largely unquantified.
source: In somatic evolution, particularly in cancer genomes, we have an extensive knowledge of the catalogue of recurrent, and likely positively selected, somatic mutations (Martincorena et al., 2017), but the fitness changes associated with each mutation remain largely unquantified.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Lineage tracing of mutations in mouse models is a prominent experimental method to determine the fitness effects of mutations.
source: Most prominently is lineage tracing of mutations in mouse models (Vermeulen et al., 2013; Rogers et al., 2018), but these methods are not sufficiently high-throughput to produce the DFE for all somatic mutations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Lineage tracing methods are not sufficiently high-throughput to produce the DFE for all somatic mutations.
source: Most prominently is lineage tracing of mutations in mouse models (Vermeulen et al., 2013; Rogers et al., 2018), but these methods are not sufficiently high-throughput to produce the DFE for all somatic mutations.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of existing methods.

claim: Some studies have estimated the selective coefficient of somatic mutations by measuring their frequency over time in the same individual using longitudinal sampling.
source: Other studies have estimated the selective coefficient of somatic mutations by measuring their frequency over time in the same individual using longitudinal sampling (Körber et al., 2019), however this method is broadly limited to somatic evolution in the blood (Gibson and Steensma, 2018) (where it is feasible to take samples from healthy individuals over time) and in rare cases of patients under active surveillance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Longitudinal sampling methods for estimating selective coefficients are broadly limited to somatic evolution in the blood and rare cases of patients under active surveillance.
source: Other studies have estimated the selective coefficient of somatic mutations by measuring their frequency over time in the same individual using longitudinal sampling (Körber et al., 2019), however this method is broadly limited to somatic evolution in the blood (Gibson and Steensma, 2018) (where it is feasible to take samples from healthy individuals over time) and in rare cases of patients under active surveillance.
evidence: This is an assessment of the practical limitations of longitudinal sampling methods, supported by citations.

claim: Methods to identify positively-selected (driver) mutations rely on finding genes that have significantly more mutational 'hits' than would be expected by chance, after correction for factors known to influence the mutation rate across the genome.
source: Methods to identify positively-selected (driver) mutations rely on finding genes that have significantly more mutational 'hits' (typically hits are non-synonymous mutations) than would be expected by chance, after correction for factors known to influence the mutation rate across the genome (Bailey et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes established methodology in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Negatively selected genes are expected to show a paucity of mutations.
source: Conversely, negatively selected genes are expected to show a paucity of mutations (Weghorn and Sunyaev, 2017; Zapata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation supported by citations to relevant work.

claim: The dN/dS ratio method was originally developed in molecular species evolution.
source: This idea is formalised in the calculation of the dN/dS ratio – a method originally developed in molecular species evolution – that has recently been adapted to study somatic evolution (both cancer and normal tissue) (Martincorena et al., 2017; Weghorn and Sunyaev, 2017; Zapata et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Greenman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003; Martincorena et al., 2018; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the origin of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The dN/dS ratio method has recently been adapted to study somatic evolution in both cancer and normal tissue.
source: This idea is formalised in the calculation of the dN/dS ratio – a method originally developed in molecular species evolution – that has recently been adapted to study somatic evolution (both cancer and normal tissue) (Martincorena et al., 2017; Weghorn and Sunyaev, 2017; Zapata et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2016; Greenman et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2003; Martincorena et al., 2018; Lee-Six et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent work.

claim: dN/dS >1 indicates positive selection.
source: The ratio of these two numbers, each normalised for the local sequence-specific biases in the mutation rate, putatively identifies a signature of selection: dN/dS >1 indicating positive selection, dN/dS = 1 indicating neutral evolution and dN/dS <1 indicating negative selection.
evidence: This is an established interpretation in the field.

claim: dN/dS = 1 indicates neutral evolution.
source: The ratio of these two numbers, each normalised for the local sequence-specific biases in the mutation rate, putatively identifies a signature of selection: dN/dS >1 indicating positive selection, dN/dS = 1 indicating neutral evolution and dN/dS <1 indicating negative selection.
evidence: This is an established interpretation in the field.

claim: dN/dS <1 indicates negative selection.
source: The ratio of these two numbers, each normalised for the local sequence-specific biases in the mutation rate, putatively identifies a signature of selection: dN/dS >1 indicating positive selection, dN/dS = 1 indicating neutral evolution and dN/dS <1 indicating negative selection.
evidence: This is an established interpretation in the field.

claim: Transforming dN/dS values to selective coefficients in somatic evolution is an unaddressed problem.
source: Transforming dN/dS values to selective coefficients in somatic evolution is an unaddressed problem.
evidence: This identifies the key gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: dN/dS was originally developed in the context of species evolution using the Wright-Fisher process.
source: dN/dS was originally developed in the context of species evolution using the Wright-Fisher process, a classical population genetics model that assumes that evolution occurs over very long timescales, which permits new mutations to fix within lineages.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the development of the method.

claim: The Wright-Fisher model assumes constant population sizes, non-overlapping generations and that all individuals have equal potency.
source: The Wright-Fisher model assumes constant population sizes, non-overlapping generations and that all individuals have equal potency.
evidence: This describes the assumptions of a classical population genetics model.

claim: In somatic evolution the assumptions of the Fisher-Wright model are violated.
source: However, in somatic evolution the assumptions of the Fisher-Wright model are violated.
evidence: This is a key observation that motivates the development of new theory in this study.

claim: Somatic evolution is rapid and new mutations are infrequently fixed in the population.
source: Somatic evolution is rapid and new mutations are infrequently fixed in the population (McGranahan and Swanton, 2017), clonal dynamics are complex (Williams et al., 2019), and population sizes unlikely to be constant (Sottoriva et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Clonal dynamics in somatic evolution are complex.
source: Somatic evolution is rapid and new mutations are infrequently fixed in the population (McGranahan and Swanton, 2017), clonal dynamics are complex (Williams et al., 2019), and population sizes unlikely to be constant (Sottoriva et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: Population sizes in somatic evolution are unlikely to be constant.
source: Somatic evolution is rapid and new mutations are infrequently fixed in the population (McGranahan and Swanton, 2017), clonal dynamics are complex (Williams et al., 2019), and population sizes unlikely to be constant (Sottoriva et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: The lack of recombination in somatic evolution can result in strong hitchhiking effects.
source: Further, the lack of recombination in somatic evolution can result in strong hitchhiking effects (Tilk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: In somatic evolution, the ancestral genome is known, which circumvents the need to measure dN/dS across a phylogeny.
source: In addition, since in somatic evolution, the ancestral genome is known, the need to measure dN/dS across a phylogeny is circumvented (a necessary step for dN/dS analysis in species evolution).
evidence: This is a key difference between somatic and species evolution that simplifies the analysis.

claim: Violations of Wright-Fisher assumptions make the interpretation of dN/dS problematic.
source: Violations of some of these assumptions was previously recognised to make the interpretation of dN/dS problematic (Kryazhimskiy and Plotkin, 2008; Mugal et al., 2014), and consequently the relationship between selective coefficients and dN/dS values is uncertain.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relationship between selective coefficients and dN/dS values is uncertain.
source: Violations of some of these assumptions was previously recognised to make the interpretation of dN/dS problematic (Kryazhimskiy and Plotkin, 2008; Mugal et al., 2014), and consequently the relationship between selective coefficients and dN/dS values is uncertain.
evidence: This identifies the key problem that the study addresses.

claim: The size distribution of clones contains information on the selective coefficients of newly arising mutations.
source: The size distribution of clones (called the site frequency spectrum in population genetics nomenclature) also contains information on the selective coefficients of newly arising mutations.
evidence: This is a theoretical insight from population genetics.

claim: Mathematical descriptions of the dynamics of populations of cells can make predictions on the shape of the clone size distribution under different demographic and evolutionary models.
source: Mathematical descriptions of the dynamics of populations of cells can make predictions on the shape of the clone size distribution under different demographic and evolutionary models (Simons, 2016a; Durrett, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: This approach has been used to quantify the dynamics and cell fate properties of stem cells across many tissues in model systems.
source: This approach has been used to quantify the dynamics and cell fate properties of stem cells across many tissues in model systems (Klein et al., 2010; Lopez-Garcia et al., 2010; Vermeulen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Similar approaches have been applied to deep sequencing data to infer the evolutionary dynamics of tumours.
source: We and others have also used similar approaches applied to deep sequencing data to infer the evolutionary dynamics of tumours (Williams et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2018; Bozic et al., 2016; Ling et al., 2015) and of clonal haematopoiesis in the blood (Watson et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: dN/dS analysis and the analysis of the clone size distribution have been performed independently, with conflictual results.
source: To date, dN/dS analysis and the analysis of the clone size distribution have been performed independently, with conflictual results (Simons, 2016b; Martincorena et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and identifies a problem in the field.

claim: The study develops mathematical population genetics theory to combine dN/dS analysis with clone size distribution analysis.
source: Here we develop the mathematical population genetics theory necessary to combine these approaches and explore how the inter-individual measure of selection at a locus as provided by dN/dS values, is related to the underlying cell population dynamics that generate intra-individual clone size distributions.
evidence: This describes the theoretical contribution of the study.

claim: The unified approach naturally accounts for the nuances in somatic evolution that can make the interpretation of dN/dS difficult.
source: This approach naturally accounts for the nuances in somatic evolution that can make the interpretation of dN/dS difficult.
evidence: This is a claimed advantage of the new approach.

claim: The study reveals the precise mathematical relationship between dN/dS values and selective coefficients in somatic evolution.
source: We show how this unified approach allows for greater insight into patterns of selection than either method in isolation, and importantly reveal the precise mathematical relationship between dN/dS values and selective coefficients in somatic evolution.
evidence: This is a primary theoretical contribution of the study.

claim: The study uses the approach to infer the selective advantage of mutations in normal tissue.
source: We use this approach to infer the selective advantage of mutations in normal tissue.
evidence: This describes the application of the method to real data.

claim: Positive selection causes selected variants to rise to higher frequency than expected under neutral evolution.
source: Positive selection causes selected variants to rise to higher frequency than expected under neutral evolution (Figure 1a), and negative selection has the opposite effect.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of population genetics, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: Negative selection causes selected variants to be at lower frequency than expected under neutral evolution.
source: Positive selection causes selected variants to rise to higher frequency than expected under neutral evolution (Figure 1a), and negative selection has the opposite effect.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of population genetics.

claim: Real sequencing data often suffers from a limited number of mutations detected at any particular frequency and measurement uncertainties in these frequencies.
source: Real sequencing data often suffers from a limited number of mutations detected at any particular frequency and measurement uncertainties in these frequencies.
evidence: This is a practical observation about limitations of sequencing data.

claim: Interval dN/dS (i-dN/dS) aggregates over a frequency range to reduce the influence of noise in sequencing data.
source: To circumvent these issues, we introduce 'interval dN/dS' (i-dN/dS) that aggregates over a frequency range to reduce the influence of these sources of noise.
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation introduced in the study.

claim: In healthy tissue, only mutations that are acquired in the stem cells will persist over long times.
source: In healthy tissue, only mutations that are acquired in the stem cells will persist over long times, and so we restrict our attention to these cells.
evidence: This is a biological principle that justifies focusing on stem cells.

claim: Quantitative analysis of lineage tracing data has shown that the stem cell dynamics of many tissues conform to a process of population asymmetry.
source: Quantitative analysis of lineage tracing data has shown that the stem cell dynamics of many tissues conform to a process of population asymmetry (Klein and Simons, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Under homeostasis, the loss of stem cells through differentiation is compensated by the replication of a neighbouring stem cell, thus maintaining an approximately constant number of stem cells.
source: In this paradigm, under homeostasis, the loss of stem cells through differentiation is compensated by the replication of a neighbouring stem cell, thus maintaining an approximately constant number of stem cells.
evidence: This describes the population asymmetry model of stem cell dynamics.

claim: The population asymmetry model is a good description of the clonal dynamics in the oesophagus and skin.
source: Previous mathematical analysis shows that this model is a good description of the clonal dynamics in the oesophagus and skin (Klein et al., 2010; Doupé et al., 2012; Alcolea et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The accuracy of the derivation was confirmed using simulations.
source: We confirmed the accuracy of our derivation using simulations (Figure 2a), and performed power calculations to determine the minimum number of mutations required to correctly infer the underlying population dynamics: we determined that 8 mutations per gene was sufficient to accurately recover Δ (Figure 2b) with accuracy increasing for higher mutation burdens (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a validation of the theoretical model using simulations, shown in Figure 2.

claim: 8 mutations per gene is sufficient to accurately recover the bias parameter Δ.
source: we determined that 8 mutations per gene was sufficient to accurately recover Δ (Figure 2b) with accuracy increasing for higher mutation burdens (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Accuracy of recovering Δ increases for higher mutation burdens.
source: we determined that 8 mutations per gene was sufficient to accurately recover Δ (Figure 2b) with accuracy increasing for higher mutation burdens (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Fitting i-dN/dS when Δ is exponentially distributed recovers the mean value of the exponential distribution on average.
source: We also performed simulations where Δ was itself a random variable, simulating the effect of different sites within the gene having different fitness effects. We assumed Δ was exponentially distributed and generated 500 simulated cohorts. Fitting i-dN/dS demonstrated that on average we infer the mean value of the exponential distribution, Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The study inferred the selective advantage of driver mutations in human oesophagus using published deep sequencing data from Martincorena and colleagues.
source: We inferred the selective advantage of driver mutations in human oesophagus using published deep sequencing data from Martincorena and colleagues (Martincorena et al., 2018) that documents the clonal expansion of a panel of putative driver mutations in histopathologically-normal oesophageal biopsies.
evidence: This describes the data source used for the analysis.

claim: dN/dS values varied considerably as a function of mutation area in the oesophagus data.
source: dN/dS values varied considerably as a function of mutation area (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The theoretical model of i-dN/dS fitted strikingly well to the oesophagus data.
source: Our theoretical model of i-dN/dS calculated from these data fitted strikingly well (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from fitting the model to data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nonsense mutations in oesophagus caused a five-fold greater bias towards self-renewal of 0.021 (0.008 – 0.032 95% CI) compared to missense mutations.
source: Nonsense mutations caused a five-fold greater bias towards self-renewal of 0.021 (0.008 – 0.032 95% CI) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: After removal of all genes that are strongly selected, global dN/dS values on the remaining 48 genes show dN/dS of approximately 1 across the frequency range.
source: After removal of all genes that are strongly selected, global dN/dS values on the remaining 48 genes show dN/dS of approximately 1 across the frequency range (Figure 2d), and i-dN/dS analysis revealed that these somatic mutations do not associate with a proliferative bias (Δ=0).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Somatic mutations in the remaining 48 genes (after removal of strongly selected genes) do not associate with a proliferative bias (Δ=0).
source: After removal of all genes that are strongly selected, global dN/dS values on the remaining 48 genes show dN/dS of approximately 1 across the frequency range (Figure 2d), and i-dN/dS analysis revealed that these somatic mutations do not associate with a proliferative bias (Δ=0).
evidence: This is a finding from the i-dN/dS analysis.

claim: A broad range of selective advantages were inferred for different genes in oesophagus.
source: We then fitted the data on a gene-by-gene and patient-by-patient basis for cases where sufficient mutations were available to perform the fit (Figure 2e–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 4). A broad range of selective advantages were inferred (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the gene-by-gene analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Mutations in TP53 showed large biases across all patients for both missense (Δ = 0.057, 95% CI: 0.05–0.068) and nonsense mutations (Δ = 0.094, 95% CI: 0.091–0.097) in oesophagus.
source: Mutations in TP53 showed large biases across all patients for both missense, Δ = 0.057 (0.05–0.068 95% CI) and nonsense mutations, Δ = 0.094 (0.091–0.097 95% CI) (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Mutations in NOTCH1 showed biases of Δ = 0.029 (95% CI: 0.019–0.036) for missense and Δ = 0.072 (95% CI: 0.034–0.089) for nonsense mutations in oesophagus.
source: This was also true for mutations in NOTCH1 with Δ = 0.029 (0.019–0.036 95% CI) for missense and Δ = 0.072 (0.034–0.089 95% CI) for nonsense mutations.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: NOTCH2, PIK3CA, CREBBP and FAT1 showed a bias toward self-proliferation in multiple patients in oesophagus.
source: NOTCH2, PIK3CA, CREBBP and FAT1 also showed a bias toward self-proliferation in multiple patients (Figure 3a–b), though most had a small effect on fitness (range 0.003–0.029 for missense mutations and 0.030–0.041 for nonsense mutations).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Most mutations in NOTCH2, PIK3CA, CREBBP and FAT1 had a small effect on fitness (range 0.003–0.029 for missense mutations and 0.030–0.041 for nonsense mutations) in oesophagus.
source: NOTCH2, PIK3CA, CREBBP and FAT1 also showed a bias toward self-proliferation in multiple patients (Figure 3a–b), though most had a small effect on fitness (range 0.003–0.029 for missense mutations and 0.030–0.041 for nonsense mutations).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis.

claim: The data suggest a distribution of fitness effects (DFE) characterized by many small effect mutations with few large effect mutations.
source: Together these data suggest a distribution of fitness effects (DFE) characterized by many small effect mutations with few large effect mutations (Figure 3c–d), as is seen in organismal evolution (Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings shown in Figure 3c-d, supported by comparison to organismal evolution.

claim: There may be intra-gene variation of selection coefficients, with some sites within genes having stronger fitness effects than others.
source: We recognize that there may be intra-gene variation of selection coefficients, that is, some sites within genes may have stronger fitness effects than others. This is supported by clustering of mutations within particular domains and hotspots of mutations as documented in the original study (Martincorena et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation, supported by citation to the original data source.

claim: Approximately 90 patches were sampled from each patient in the oesophagus study.
source: Approximately 90 patches were sampled from each patient.
evidence: This describes the sampling design of the original study.

claim: There was a statistically significant correlation between the number of driver mutations per patch and the number of synonymous mutations for both NOTCH1 (p<0.001) and TP53 mutations (p=0.031).
source: While there =was a statistically significant correlation for both NOTCH1 (linear regression, p<0.001) and TP53 mutations (p=0.031), the effect was small (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): for each additional driver there was on average 0.05 additional synonymous variants (0.047 for NOTCH1 and 0.056 for TP53).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hitchhiking analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For each additional driver mutation there was on average 0.05 additional synonymous variants (0.047 for NOTCH1 and 0.056 for TP53).
source: While there =was a statistically significant correlation for both NOTCH1 (linear regression, p<0.001) and TP53 mutations (p=0.031), the effect was small (Figure 5—figure supplement 1): for each additional driver there was on average 0.05 additional synonymous variants (0.047 for NOTCH1 and 0.056 for TP53).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the hitchhiking analysis.

claim: The correlation between driver mutations and synonymous mutations was very noisy (R2 < 0.02).
source: We note too that the correlation was very noisy (R2 < 0.02) and we observed no statistically significant relationship between VAF of synonymous mutations and the number of TP53 or NOTCH1 mutations (linear regression, p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hitchhiking analysis.

claim: There was no statistically significant relationship between VAF of synonymous mutations and the number of TP53 or NOTCH1 mutations (p>0.1).
source: We note too that the correlation was very noisy (R2 < 0.02) and we observed no statistically significant relationship between VAF of synonymous mutations and the number of TP53 or NOTCH1 mutations (linear regression, p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hitchhiking analysis.

claim: The analysis suggests that the majority of synonymous mutations are not hitchhikers.
source: This analysis suggests that the majority of synonymous mutations are not hitchhikers, and consequently that assuming the independence of clones isreasonable.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the hitchhiking analysis results.

claim: Assuming the independence of clones is reasonable for the oesophagus data.
source: This analysis suggests that the majority of synonymous mutations are not hitchhikers, and consequently that assuming the independence of clones isreasonable.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the hitchhiking analysis that validates a model assumption.

claim: The per-patient average selective advantage per mutation in normal skin is Δ = 0.001 for missense mutations.
source: Analyses of these data with interval dN/dS revealed a per-patient average selective advantage per mutation (again measured in terms of the bias towards self renewal) of Δ = 0.001 for missense mutations and four-fold higher (Δ = ﻿0.004) for nonsense mutations (Figure 4a-c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the skin data analysis shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: The per-patient average selective advantage per mutation in normal skin is Δ = 0.004 for nonsense mutations, four-fold higher than missense mutations.
source: Analyses of these data with interval dN/dS revealed a per-patient average selective advantage per mutation (again measured in terms of the bias towards self renewal) of Δ = 0.001 for missense mutations and four-fold higher (Δ = ﻿0.004) for nonsense mutations (Figure 4a-c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the skin data analysis shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Good fits to the skin data were obtainable for NOTCH1 missense mutations in patient PD18003 with fitness estimated to be Δ = 0.0149 (95% CI: 0.0148-0.0150).
source: Good fits to the data were obtainable for NOTCH1 missense mutations in patient PD18003 with fitness estimated to be Δ = 0.0149 (0.0148-0.0150 95% CI), and TP53 missense mutations also in patient PD18003, Δ = 0.0054 (0.0051-0.0058 95% CI) Figure 4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the gene-level analysis in skin shown in Figure 4.

claim: Good fits to the skin data were obtainable for TP53 missense mutations in patient PD18003 with fitness estimated to be Δ = 0.0054 (95% CI: 0.0051-0.0058).
source: Good fits to the data were obtainable for NOTCH1 missense mutations in patient PD18003 with fitness estimated to be Δ = 0.0149 (0.0148-0.0150 95% CI), and TP53 missense mutations also in patient PD18003, Δ = 0.0054 (0.0051-0.0058 95% CI) Figure 4.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the gene-level analysis in skin shown in Figure 4.

claim: The fitness coefficients for NOTCH1 and TP53 in skin were similar to the oesophagus data.
source: These fitness coefficients were similar to the oesophagus data.
evidence: This is a comparison between the skin and oesophagus findings.

claim: The distribution of fitness effects for missense mutations in skin showed similar characteristics to the oesophagus data of a small number of high effect mutations and a larger number of smaller effect mutations.
source: For missense mutations we were also able to produce the distribution of fitness effects across the skin cohort, which showed similar characteristics to the oesophagus data of a small number of high effect mutations and a larger number of smaller effect mutations, Figure 4f.
evidence: This is a finding from the DFE analysis in skin shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Plotting the distribution of clone size areas showed a widening of the distribution as a function of age.
source: Plotting the distribution of clone size areas showed a widening of the distribution as a function of age, which was particularly striking for mutations in the NOTCH1 and TP53 genes, consistent with these genes conferring large selective advantages (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an observation from the site frequency spectrum analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The widening of the clone size distribution as a function of age was particularly striking for mutations in the NOTCH1 and TP53 genes, consistent with these genes conferring large selective advantages.
source: Plotting the distribution of clone size areas showed a widening of the distribution as a function of age, which was particularly striking for mutations in the NOTCH1 and TP53 genes, consistent with these genes conferring large selective advantages (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is an observation from the site frequency spectrum analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Using WAIC to perform model selection, a model with an exponential term and a power law was found to be the best fitting model (lowest WAIC).
source: Using WAIC to perform model selection, we found a model with an exponential term and a power law to be the best fitting model (lowest WAIC).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Posterior estimates of the characteristic frequency N(t) showed an increase as a function of age for non-synonymous mutations and a more modest increase for synonymous mutations.
source: Posterior estimates of the characteristic frequency N(t) showed an increase as a function of age for non-synonymous mutations and a more modest increase for synonymous as would be predicted from theory, Figure 5d.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian fitting shown in Figure 5d, consistent with theoretical predictions.

claim: Bayes factors for the proposed theoretical model strongly supported it as the best model (BF > 10³ for both alternative models).
source: Bayes factors for the proposed theoretical model also strongly supported this as the best model (BF > 103 for both models).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison.

claim: Bayesian multi-level regression revealed that TP53 and NOTCH1 had the largest regression coefficients, consistent with these genes having the largest selection coefficients.
source: As an alternative to fitting the full clone size distribution, we performed a Bayesian multi-level regression to assess which mutations showed the largest increase in clone size as a function of age. This analysis revealed that TP53 and NOTCH1 had the largest regression coefficients, consistent with these genes having the largest selection coefficients, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, providing qualitative support for our approach.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inferred selection coefficients from i-dN/dS were correlated with the regression coefficients from the statistical model (linear regression, p=0.004, R² = 0.47).

evidence: This is a statistical finding showing consistency between different analytical approaches.

claim: The proposed model provides the best fit to data when compared to other similar models.
source: Taken together, analysis of the site frequency spectrum on a patient by patient basis and a gene level statistical model are consistent with our inferences from i-dN/dS. We find that the proposed model provides the best fit to data when compared to other similar models, that the characteristic frequency of non-synonymous mutations increases rapidly with age and that NOTCH1 and TP53 exhibit the largest increase in clone size as a function of age.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the site frequency spectrum analysis.

source: We note that our study also shows that the magnitude of the selection coefficient is not necessarily represented by simply calculating a 'point estimate' of dN/dS that neglects mutation subclonal frequency information.

claim: In both skin and oesophagus, the most highly selected mutant genes were NOTCH1 and TP53 (increased proliferative bias of >1% and >5% respectively).

source: This consistency in selective coefficients is in agreement with the observation of highly recurrent gene mutations in cancer (Lawrence et al., 2013) and evidence of repeatability in cancer evolution (Caravagna et al., 2018).

source: Non-synonymous NOTCH1 mutations were observed approximately 3-fold more frequently that non-synonymous TP53 mutations in oesophagus, and approximately 5-fold more frequently in skin, suggesting that the mutation rate of NOTCH1 is greater than for TP53.

claim: The oesophagus will become transiently repopulated by NOTCH1-mutant cells during ageing, before subsequent replacement by fitter mutant-TP53 clones.
source: Coupling these data with our quantitative measurements of the fitness coefficients leads to the prediction that the oesophagus will become transiently repopulated by NOTCH1-mutant cells during ageing, before subsequent replacement by fitter mutant-TP53 clones.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the combination of mutation rates and fitness coefficients.

claim: The clonality of mutations strongly determine the observed value of dN/dS.
source: On a cautionary note, our theoretical work shows that the clonality of mutations strongly determine the observed value of dN/dS, and so a misleading picture of the selective forces will be produced if dN/dS frequency-dependent effects are not corrected for.
evidence: This is a theoretical insight from the study.

claim: The accuracy of any estimate of evolutionary dynamics from dN/dS values is dependent on the underlying accuracy of the dN/dS measure itself.
source: The accuracy of any estimate of evolutionary dynamics from dN/dS values is of course dependent on the underlying accuracy of the dN/dS measure itself, which is compromised by uncharacterised variability in the mutation rate across the genome (Van den Eynden and Larsson, 2017) and in the uncertain pathogenicity of individual single nucleotide variants (extensions to estimate site level selection coefficients may circumvent some of these issues [Cannataro et al., 2018; Temko et al., 2018]).
evidence: This acknowledges limitations of the approach, supported by citations.

claim: The model assumes a well-mixed population, while the data used in the study is from spatially structured epithelia.
source: We also recognize that our model assumes a well-mixed population, while the data used in our study is from spatially structured epithelia.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the model.

claim: Spatial structure influences the distribution of clone sizes.
source: Spatial structure influences the distribution of clone sizes. Effects include: the influence of the boundary that enable rapid growth of mutants on the expanding front and conversely 'encapsulation' within a growing mass that slows clone growth (Fusco et al., 2016; Chkhaidze et al., 2019), and clonal interference that slows the growth of two similarly fit competing clones (Martens et al., 2011; Hall et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to relevant work.

claim: Combining population genetics methods with comparative genomics is a powerful way to infer selection pressures in human somatic evolution.
source: Combining population genetics methods with comparative genomics is a powerful way to infer selection pressures in human somatic evolution, giving new insight into the fundamental parameters that determine evolutionary dynamics in health and disease.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the value of the approach.
